packs.title: Light, Stone & Green Paths
packs.promise: Follow changing light, try small inventions and find a quieter pace across Reykjavík.

q.s: Give one small fictional moment a beginning and an ending.
st: From an open path or comfortable resting place, choose one real park detail: a branching path, a tree or an empty stretch of lawn.
Invent a small event that could start there, such as a lost mitten being noticed. Do not use a stranger as your character.
Make three panels or three sentences: before, a change, and after. Let your chosen detail matter in the middle part.
Give the ending a gentle surprise. Label the story as your invention; no performance or photograph is required.

q.s: Test what changes when you move, and what stays put.
st: From the forecourt or an open public foyer, find a pane that reflects sky, one that reveals something behind it and one that looks darker. One pane may do more than one job.
Choose a single pane and predict what a small change of viewing position will do.
Move a few safe steps, or change your viewing angle from a seated position. Check your prediction without blocking a doorway.
Record the three effects and whether your chosen pane changed. A cloudy day is a valid result; bright colour is not required.

q.s: Make a rule, then find a plant that tests it.
st: Find three plants from open paths. Use visible leaves, needles, branching, bark or seed shapes; flowers are not required.
Make a two-question key using clear differences such as rounded or narrow, smooth or ridged. Draw the choices or describe them in words.
Test the key on a fourth plant. If it fits badly, improve one question instead of forcing the plant into a category.
Record the revised key. Use names only when a readable label supports them, and leave all material growing where it is.

packs.title: Pond & Old Town
packs.promise: Find small stories between Reykjavík’s pond, old lanes and harbour edge.

q.s: Let a relief model turn flat names into landforms.
st: At an open viewing side of the Iceland model, choose a peninsula, a valley-like low area and a high area by their visible forms. Read labels only if they are clear.
Follow an imaginary line between two of those forms with your eyes. Decide where your invented line would bend to avoid high ground.
Find one place where the model leaves you uncertain about what a traveler would encounter.
Record the three forms, one imagined bend and the uncertainty. This is a model-reading exercise, not an actual travel route.

q.s: Separate a visible clue from what you think it means.
st: Choose one part of the preserved excavation or one labeled object that you can comfortably see.
Record a direct observation without explaining it yet: material, shape, position or a readable label detail.
Read the museum’s interpretation. Add one supported statement about how the object or structure was used.
Make a three-part evidence card: what I observed, what the museum explains, and one question still open. You do not need to solve the question.

q.s: Give a harbour building an invented two-scene story.
st: From a safe public place by the museum, choose one window, opening or part of the exterior that catches your attention.
Read the museum’s short building history: Hafnarhús was used for harbour operations and storage before becoming an art museum.
Invent two scenes around an imaginary empty box: one in its warehouse past and one in its museum present. Draw them or write two short paragraphs.
Keep your fiction separate from the sourced building history. The box and its journey are yours; no real exhibit or former worker is being described.
